interviewQuestions.question: How would you convince leadership to invest in a costly re-architecture?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd translate the technical problem into terms leadership already tracks — cost, risk, or speed — with real numbers, rather than arguing that the current architecture is bad engineering. For example, instead of "our monolith is hard to maintain," I'd present "we've had 6 Sev1 outages this quarter, each costing an estimated $50K in lost transactions, and our postmortems trace 4 of them to the same coupling problem this re-architecture fixes."

Where possible, I'd tie the ask to a business initiative leadership already wants — "our current database can't support next year's multi-region expansion; without this migration, that roadmap item isn't achievable at all, not just slower" — which reframes the ask from new spend to unblocking a commitment.

I'd propose a phased plan with a cheaper first milestone that delivers partial value quickly, rather than asking for the full multi-quarter budget upfront with no visible progress until the end.

**Testing:** whether you can make a business case in terms non-technical stakeholders act on, not just a technical justification.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Building the business case for a re-architecture

interviewQuestions.question: You got the budget for the re-architecture, but six months in, a critical feature deadline threatens to pull the team off it — how do you protect it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd use the same tool teams use for reliability error budgets: pre-agree, before the pressure ever hits, on what a temporary pause looks like versus an outright cancellation, and on protecting at minimum whatever milestone is already in flight rather than letting the whole effort unwind.

Concretely, that means at the time I originally pitched the phased plan, I'd have already gotten agreement that a pause preserves the completed milestones and picks back up at the next checkpoint, rather than the project restarting from scratch or being silently abandoned. That agreement, made calmly before any real conflict exists, is far more durable than trying to negotiate protection for the project in the middle of a heated deadline crunch.

When the feature deadline actually arrives, I'd point back to that pre-agreement rather than re-litigating the re-architecture's value from scratch under time pressure.

**Testing:** whether you can protect a long-term investment against short-term pressure using an agreement made in advance, rather than defending it reactively in the moment.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Protecting the re-architecture from a competing deadline

interviewQuestions.question: How do you adjust your pitch when talking to an engineering-heavy audience versus a purely business-focused one?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd keep the same underlying facts but shift which parts I lead with. For a business-focused audience, I'd lead with the quantified cost of the status quo and the opportunity cost of not acting — real dollar figures and roadmap impact — and keep the technical detail available but secondary. For an engineering-heavy audience, I'd lead with the specific technical root cause and why the proposed architecture actually fixes it, since they can evaluate execution risk that a purely business framing would gloss over.

I'd avoid the trap of using only one framing for both audiences: pure business language risks oversimplifying technical nuance that the engineering audience needs to trust the plan will actually work, while pure technical language risks losing the audience that controls the budget entirely.

In practice, most real pitches have both audiences in the room at once, so I'd structure the pitch with the business case up front and the technical justification available in appendix-level depth for whoever needs to dig in.

**Testing:** whether you can adapt the same underlying case to different audiences without changing the facts or losing either audience.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Adapting the pitch to different audiences
